findings.title: Sign out everywhere leaves every phone’s push token: a lost phone keeps getting the person’s pushes
findings.detail: D142 (5) makes a push token one person’s and says sign-out deletes it, *because a stale token would show someone’s notifications on a phone they’ve left*. The lost-phone journey (flows.md) is exactly that phone: from another device, Settings → Account → *Sign out everywhere*. `apiAuth.signOutEverywhere()` calls `letGo()`, whose `stopPush()` deletes only **this** device’s token (and only when push started in this session), then `/auth/revoke-sessions` revokes every session but touches no `push_tokens` row. Every other phone keeps its token, so the scheduler’s pushes (today the backup and storage alerts; later the check-in, claim reminders and the rest) keep arriving on the lost phone. Nothing on the server deletes a person’s tokens when their sessions are revoked.
findings.repro: API on sen_qa (qa/e2e/b06.config.ts header). Sign in as qa-ben; PUT /api/push/token with four tokens; POST /api/auth/revoke-sessions; count push_tokens for Ben.

findings.title: The test push and test job routes are open to every member, not the admin only
findings.detail: D142 (4): *Production’s test menu is Settings → Data’s Checks, admin only: Send a test push and Schedule a test job, 3 a minute at most.* The screen hides *Checks* from a member, but `POST /api/push/test` and `POST /api/jobs/test` are mounted in `personJobRoutes` with access `person` (routes.table.ts), with a rate limit and no admin check. Any signed-in member can schedule test jobs (each one wakes the Worker and then the API and Neon at its minute, D141) and send test pushes. `apps/api/test/jobs.test.ts` asserts the member *can* (`schedules the test job … cookie: cookies.member` → 200), so the suite pins the deviation rather than the decision.

findings.title: Any member can make /health/jobs green with their own job_runs rows (a fake backup and morning run)
findings.detail: `record_backup()` is owner-only so that only `sen_ops`’ workflow can record a backup (D142 (2), §17 *Only migrations and the backup use the owner role*), and pgTAP checks the API’s role can’t call it. But 0008 grants `INSERT, UPDATE` on `job_runs` to `app_user`, and RLS lets a person write their own rows with any `job` and `status`, while `jobs_health()` reads `max(ran_at)` of `job = 'backup' and status = 'ok'` across **everyone**. So one `app_user` statement as any member hides a dead backup from the outside monitor. No route exposes job_runs today, so it needs SQL as app_user (a future generic resource route or an injection); defence in depth for the one guard that tells the owner backups stopped. Narrow it: let `jobs_health()` count only the admin’s backup rows, or refuse `job = 'backup'` in the insert policy.

findings.title: The test that should hold “polling stops once the relay is back” can’t see polling continue
findings.detail: realtime.test.ts *reloads only the active queries every 30 s, and reconnecting reloads everything and stops that* checks for no invalidation within `PING_MS - 1` (25 s) after the reconnect. The 30 s interval started when the relay dropped, so its next fire after a reconnect at ~30 s is ~60 s, outside the window. Deleting `stopPolling()` from `onopen` leaves the suite green (probe P9). The behaviour itself is right today (FLOW-2 step 4: 0 settings reads in 35 s once live), but a regression that polls every open screen every 30 s forever (keeping Neon awake, D141’s whole point) would pass CI.
findings.repro: In apps/web/src/data/realtime.ts delete the line `      stopPolling();` in `s.onopen`; `pnpm exec vitest run apps/web/src/data/realtime.test.ts`.
findings.spec: AC-35; brief “every 30 s only while the relay is down”; D100

findings.title: Schedule a test job promises a push that may never come
findings.detail: The eyes pass (qa/B06/eyes.md, entry 5, *wrong*): the toast says *Test job set for 16:54. Its push arrives then.* on a device that a moment earlier was told *Push isn’t set up here.*, or that has no phone registered at all (a browser). When the job runs, Settings → Data shows nothing new, so the owner can’t tell a job that ran from one that didn’t. `scheduleTestJob()` always promises the push; the job’s `jobs` hint invalidates only the settings query, which shows no job result.

findings.title: The stamp pushes the screen down by about 30 px when it appears and goes
findings.detail: The eyes pass (entry 7, *look again*), confirmed by measuring FLOW-2-step-2 against FLOW-2-step-3: LiveStamp is a block between the app bar and the content, so when the relay drops or returns everything below it moves by the stamp’s height, under a finger that may be about to tap a payday choice. findings.title: A person who knows another’s FCM token can take it
findings.detail: `push_token_claim()` moves a token to whoever claims it (D142 (5), by design), so a member who learnt another person’s token would receive that person’s pushes. Tokens never leave the phone or the server, so this is a note on the design’s trust in the token, not a defect.
findings.repro: As Ben: PUT /api/push/token {"token":"tok-a"} (the admin’s seeded token).

findings.title: The tick’s own database work isn’t in its Server-Timing
findings.detail: The route sweep’s metrics show `POST /api/jobs/tick 200` with 2 queries, but a tick runs `jobs_people`, a claim, a finish and each task per person through `deps.pool`, outside the request’s counted connection. When later slices add work to the frames, the tick’s cost won’t show in QA’s API metrics.
findings.evidence: POST /api/jobs/tick 200   n=2 appMs med=9.2 max=9.2 queries max=2

findings.title: Production’s CSP also admits the preview relay
findings.detail: vercel.json’s one CSP serves production and previews alike, so production’s `connect-src` includes `wss://sen-worker-preview.sen-my.workers.dev`. Connecting is all it allows and passes are signed per Worker, so nothing reaches the bridge; it is still one more origin than production needs.

findings.title: Read, not run: a wake that lands during a tick can be lost
findings.detail: By reading only (not reproduced): `Scheduler.cron()` saves `await this.tick(s, now)`, built from the state read before the tick’s fetch. A `wake()` that arrives while that fetch is in flight (the Durable Object’s input gate opens during it) is saved, then overwritten by the tick’s result. If the API scheduled the job after the tick’s own `jobs_next_once()` query, the job waits for the next frame, up to 14 hours. The window is a few milliseconds; a test job tapped at that instant would be late. Re-reading the state after the tick and keeping the earlier `next` would close it.
